USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the active negotiation track toward a comprehensive, enforceable settlement and follow through on the planned Xi-Trump summit (Mar-a-Lago) to lock in the concessions China has already offered — increased US purchases of soybeans, energy and other goods, plus a currency pledge — while keeping the deferred 10%→25% escalation on the $200B list as a credible backstop. Do not concede structural demands (IP, tech transfer, enforcement) prematurely, and do not provoke a fresh escalation that would hit US importers, consumers and the already-ailing farm belt. Hold the leverage, negotiate hard, and only roll back tariffs in exchange for written, enforceable commitments.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: This is a managed standoff trending toward a deal, and it reads as a slight opportunity for the US rather than a threat. The US entered the negotiation holding the leverage: it imposed 25% tariffs on $50B of Chinese goods and 10% on ~$200B (event timeline 2018-09-24), and China is the more exposed party seeking relief. Trump has already extracted real concessions — China significantly increased soybean/energy purchase commitments and agreed to a currency non-devaluation pledge in talks, and Xi agreeing to travel to Mar-a-Lago rather than Hainan is itself read as a concession (web: NYT 2019-02-24). The tariff hike was deferred (timeline 2019-02-24) and the March 1 deadline passed without escalation, reflecting substantive-but-incomplete progress. Tempering the opportunity is genuine domestic pain: China's 25% soybean import tax has driven prices to a decade low, left ~27.5M tons of US soybeans potentially unsold and ~$7.9B in farmer losses, and pushed Washington into ~$9.6B in bailouts (web: BI/USDA, SCMP). US macro is also cooling mildly — industrial production slipped from ~104 to ~102.9 and the 10Y Treasury yield fell from ~3.2% to 2.61% — so an uncontrolled escalation would be costly (country_health: INDPRO, DGS10). These factors keep the threat score only mildly negative (-0.3) rather than a clear -1.0. The action stance is therefore to negotiate (0.0): neither concede — China has still not made written commitments on the core structural/enforcement issues (web: NYT) and giving up leverage now would forfeit the main US gains — nor escalate, which would inflict self-damage and risk derailing the favorable trajectory. The disciplined move is to press for a written, enforceable deal at the summit while holding the hike as a fallback.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the trade talks constructively to lock in the pause on the List 3 tariff hike and secure a deal that rolls back existing Section 301 tariffs, while using the Huawei/Meng leverage without letting it derail the tariff track. Avoid new escalation — we cannot afford a return to the 25% List 3 hike or fresh tariff rounds on top of an already-falling export base — but do not pre-commit to sweeping structural/tech-transfer reform before concrete tariff relief is on the table. Hold our negotiating line and press for reciprocal concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential. US Section 301 tariffs now cover ~$250B of Chinese goods (List 1 $34B + List 2 $16B at 25%, List 3 $200B at 10%) and are demonstrably biting: exports plunged 20.7% y/y in February, imports fell 5.2%, and Jan–Feb exports to the US dropped ~14% (Reuters/Globe/Fox, Mar 8). That maps to the CHN '+0.5' anchor (major export sectors hit, firm-level targeting). Huawei adds a second front: the US unsealed charges and Canada voted on Mar 1 to proceed with Meng's extradition, which Beijing frames as 'political persecution' of a high-tech enterprise (NPR Mar 1/6; Politico Mar 3) — a direct threat to our tech-champion ambitions. Offsetting this are the two suspended List 3 hikes (Feb 24 and the Mar 1 deadline passing without an increase) plus credible progress signals — Wang Yi citing 'substantive progress' and Trump saying talks are 'very, very close' — so I read this as +0.4 rather than +0.5: the escalation is paused and a negotiated off-ramp is live. On action, de-escalation-by-negotiation is right: escalating would make a bad export situation worse and invite the very 25% hike we have paused, while the Huawei case already gives us leverage to keep the conversation going. A mild positive action_score (+0.1, negotiate) reflects continuing talks toward purchases and relief without premature structural concessions while enforcement and IP/tech-transfer issues remain unresolved.
